svg.title: Growing something small
svg.desc: Original family-manga illustration: plant, related to Growing something small.

text.tspan: The decision to care for a plant may appear ordinary, yet it exposes a recurring tension between arrangements that make
life manageable and experiences that resist being prescribed. A defensible approach combines proportionate preparation
with a willingness to reconsider whose interests a plan serves.
Preparation has value because observing a plant helps us respond to what it needs. In the present case, we check whether the soil feels dry before adding
water. Such an intervention is modest, but that modesty is its strength: it removes a foreseeable obstacle without claiming to determine the entire experience.
Structure is useful to the extent that it releases attention rather than consuming it.
That argument requires a qualification, however: keeping a simple record helps us learn from changes. For instance, we note which window gives the plant
enough light without scorching its leaves. An arrangement that appears efficient from one standpoint may impose costs elsewhere. Listening to those affected
is therefore not an optional gesture of goodwill; it supplies information without which the plan cannot be adequately evaluated.
The resulting principle is one of proportion. Preparation deserves support when it clarifies responsibilities and protects time, while responsiveness prevents it
from hardening into an end in itself. To judge the experience well is to examine both what the arrangement enables and what it may inadvertently exclude.
BUILD YOUR OWN · State a focused main idea. Develop one supporting reason in each body paragraph, with a concrete example. Conclude by connecting the two
reasons without introducing a new argument. Use the structure as a model; write about an experience of your own.
Explain your reasoning to a partner. What two reasons support the main idea? Explain one example.
